newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Embryo EU bank changes leaders in EMU run-up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Embryo EU bank changes leaders in EMU run-up.

text.p: Dutch central bank governor Wim Duisenberg, set to take control at the European Union's embryo central bank this week, said on Monday he hoped to lead the fully-fledged version as well.

Duisenberg will officially become the new president of the European Monetary Institute (EMI), forerunner of the future European Central Bank (ECB), on Tuesday, when he will chair his first EMI council meeting.
Belgian Alexandre Lamfalussy, the EMI's first president, marked his departure in a glamorous ceremony on Monday attended by top European bankers.

Speculation has grown that Duisenberg, a 61-year-old free-spending socialist turned hard-nosed central banker, will also be the first head of the Frankfurt-based central bank at the start of European economic and monetary union (EMU) in January 1999.

On Sunday he received a ringing endorsement from Hans Tietmeyer, president of the German Bundesbank, who said Duisenberg's selection would be a signal of commitment to stability for the new euro currency.
"I believe that Mr Duisenberg really stands for lasting stability," Tietmeyer told German radio.
"In that respect, a decision (to appoint him as ECB head) would certainly also be a signal in the right direction."

Duisenberg said on Monday he was uncertain of his chances of being appointed head of the ECB, which will be created in 1998 after initial countries qualifying for the new single currency are selected.

But he reaffirmed his desire for the job and said it was "very good" to learn of the endorsement from Tietmeyer, who will have an influential voice over how the bank will be formed due to Germany's dominant position in the potential euro zone.
Duisenberg has been widely tipped as the first president of the bank after he was chosen to take over the EMI because of his credentials as a fierce anti-inflation fighter.
But Juergen Stark, the state secretary of the German finance ministry who also attended the ceremony, declined to offer a clear endorsement.
Although he said Duisenberg was currently the only official candidate, Stark said his tenure at the EMI would be a test.
"Duisenberg now has about 12 months time or until about the end of April to fulfil the very high expectations that we have placed on him," Stark said.

Duisenberg tried to keep the focus off himself in a speech praising Lamfalussy, 68, who established the EMI in January 1994 and has been a guiding force in the debate over prospects for a single European currency.

"One of your greatest assets is that you managed to combine the typical conservative and cautious nature of a central banker, always focused on substance, with your firm belief in European monetary integration," he said of Lamfalussy.

Other European leaders praised the work of Lamfalussy, who has been credited with creating a well-received blueprint for the future central bank and for being a pragmatic voice on the challenges of currency union.

Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok said Lamfalussy played a key role in preparing for the euro and also sought to quell a growing dispute between Bonn and leaders in the German state of Bavaria over whether to delay EMU if entry rules were not strictly met.
"Hesitation now would harm the Union's cogency and credibility. Tremendous efforts have been and are being made. There is a great deal at stake. We really cannot afford to let EMU fail," Kok said.

Lamfalussy himself used his last public speech to call on European leaders to find new ways to address high unemployment, which he said was eroding the social fabric, and said monetary policy had limited power to create new jobs.
"The current level of unemployment in the majority of our countries is ethically unacceptable," Lamfalussy said. "Reducing unemployment must be the prime objective of action by authorities."
